name: Serval and Rooted Tree
description: Now Serval is a junior high school student in Japari Middle School, and he is still thrilled on math as before. As a talented boy in mathematics, he likes to play with numbers. This time, he wants to play with numbers on a rooted tree. A tree is a connected graph without cycles. A rooted tree has a special vertex called the root. A parent of a node $$$v$$$ is the last different from $$$v$$$ vertex on the path from the root to the vertex $$$v$$$. Children of vertex $$$v$$$ are all nodes for which $$$v$$$ is the parent. A vertex is a leaf if it has no children. The rooted tree Serval owns has $$$n$$$ nodes, node $$$1$$$ is the root. Serval will write some numbers into all nodes of the tree. However, there are some restrictions. Each of the nodes except leaves has an operation $$$\max$$$ or $$$\min$$$ written in it, indicating that the number in this node should be equal to the maximum or minimum of all the numbers in its sons, respectively. Assume that there are $$$k$$$ leaves in the tree. Serval wants to put integers $$$1, 2, \ldots, k$$$ to the $$$k$$$ leaves (each number should be used exactly once). He loves large numbers, so he wants to maximize the number in the root. As his best friend, can you help him?
input_specification: The first line contains an integer $$$n$$$ ($$$2 \leq n \leq 3\cdot 10^5$$$), the size of the tree. The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers, the $$$i$$$-th of them represents the operation in the node $$$i$$$. $$$0$$$ represents $$$\min$$$ and $$$1$$$ represents $$$\max$$$. If the node is a leaf, there is still a number of $$$0$$$ or $$$1$$$, but you can ignore it. The third line contains $$$n-1$$$ integers $$$f_2, f_3, \ldots, f_n$$$ ($$$1 \leq f_i \leq i-1$$$), where $$$f_i$$$ represents the parent of the node $$$i$$$.
output_specification: Output one integer — the maximum possible number in the root of the tree.
approach_summary: Define tree DP state dp[u][state] computing optimal subproblem values for the subtree rooted at u. Aggregate transitions across children in post-order traversal in O(N × S) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1153D — Serval and Rooted Tree [463. DP on Trees and DAGs]
topic_editorial.summary: Tree Dynamic Programming with post-order traversal.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: A rooted tree has a clean hierarchical structure: removing the root decomposes the tree into independent disjoint subtrees. Therefore, the optimal solution for a subtree rooted at vertex $u$ depends purely on the solutions of its direct children $v \in \text{children}(u)$.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Root Selection & State Definition
Arbitrarily root the tree at node $1$. Define:
- $dp[u][0] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is excluded.
- $dp[u][1] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is included.

### Step 2: Post-Order DFS Traversal
We traverse the tree using depth-first search. A node $u$ computes its answers only after all its children $v \in \text{adj}[u]$ have computed theirs:
$$\text{dfs}(u, \text{parent})$$

### Step 3: Subtree Transition
For each child $v$ of $u$ ($v \ne \text{parent}$):
$$dp[u][0] = \sum_{v} \max(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])$$
$$dp[u][1] = \text{val}[u] + \sum_{v} dp[v][0]$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
At the root:
$$\text{Ans} = \max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1])$$
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Each node and edge in the tree is visited exactly once during the DFS traversal. All transitions at node $u$ run in time proportional to its degree. Summing across all vertices: $\sum \text{deg}(u) = 2(N-1) = \mathcal{O}(N)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Adjacency list storage takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, DP state arrays take $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, and the DFS call stack takes at most $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth in the worst case.
